questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless, indurated ulcer with raised, undermined edges on his right forearm for 3 weeks. Gram stain shows Gram-positive filamentous organisms. Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: The clinical picture of an indurated ulcer with undermined edges in an agricultural worker with Gram-positive filamentous organisms is classic for Actinomyces israelii (actinomycosis). Actinomyces are Gram-positive, non-acid-fast, anaerobic filamentous bacteria. Nocardia is also filamentous but is weakly acid-fast and typically causes lymphocutaneous infection.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompromised patient develops painful grouped vesicles along the T5 dermatome. Three days later, new lesions appear on the contralateral side. This presentation is best described as:
questions.exp: Disseminated herpes zoster is defined as >20 vesicles outside the primary and immediately adjacent dermatomes, or involvement of visceral organs. In immunocompromised patients, zoster can disseminate hematogenously. Bilateral dermatomal involvement is characteristic of disseminated HZV. Localized zoster affects one dermatome unilaterally.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with erythematous plaques with overlying silvery scales on her elbows and knees. Biopsy shows parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, and dilated dermal capillaries. The Munro microabscess in this condition is formed by accumulation of which cells?
questions.exp: Munro microabscesses in psoriasis are collections of neutrophils within the stratum corneum/parakeratotic layer. They are pathognomonic of psoriasis. Eosinophilic spongiosis with eosinophil-rich infiltrate is seen in pemphigus. Pautrier microabscesses in mycosis fungoides are composed of atypical lymphocytes.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse presents with a painless genital ulcer for 2 weeks. Dark-field microscopy shows corkscrew motility of organisms. The causative agent produces a virulence factor that cleaves IgA antibodies. This enzyme is called:
questions.exp: The painless genital ulcer with corkscrew motility on dark-field microscopy is classic for primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. T. pallidum produces IgA1 protease which cleaves secretory IgA1, facilitating mucosal invasion. Coagulase is produced by S. aureus, hyaluronidase by streptococci, and leucocidin by S. aureus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient from Bihar presents with hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear from the lesion is negative (BI=0). Histopathology shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with scanty lymphocytes at dermoepidermal junction. What type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocyte cuffing, eroding into the epidermis at the DEJ. BI is 0 (paucibacillary). BT granulomas are less well-formed and do not touch the epidermis. BB has an ill-defined granuloma, and LL shows foamy histiocytes (Virchow cells) with numerous bacilli.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing lupus erythematosus develops painful erythematous urticarial plaques on sun-exposed areas. C3 and C4 are low, anti-C1q antibodies are elevated. What is this condition called?
questions.exp: Urticarial vasculitis in SLE (hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis) is characterized by urticarial lesions lasting >24 hours, low C3/C4, elevated anti-C1q antibodies, and leukocytoclastic vasculitis on biopsy. It is associated with systemic SLE. Rowell syndrome is discoid LE with erythema multiforme-like lesions. Schnitzler syndrome is urticarial vasculitis with IgM paraproteinemia.

questions.q: A 50-year-old patient presents with tense bullae arising on normal skin and urticarial plaques. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA for BP180 (NC16A domain) is positive. What is the most effective treatment?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is the diagnosis. Large randomized controlled trials (particularly the French RCT by Joly et al.) have shown that topical superpotent corticosteroids (clobetasol propionate 40g/day) are as effective as systemic corticosteroids but with fewer systemic side effects, making them first-line for moderate-severe BP. Rituximab is used for refractory pemphigus, not first-line BP.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient with CD4 count of 80 cells/μL develops extensive molluscum contagiosum with large umbilicated papules on the face and neck. The causative poxvirus replicates in which cellular compartment?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) is a poxvirus. All poxviruses replicate exclusively in the cytoplasm, forming characteristic eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions called Henderson-Paterson bodies (molluscum bodies). This distinguishes poxviruses from herpesviruses which replicate in the nucleus. In immunocompromised patients, giant molluscum (>1cm) and extensive disease are seen.

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient presents with white, creamy plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off easily. KOH preparation shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. Which virulence factor of the causative organism allows tissue invasion?
questions.exp: Candida albicans causes oropharyngeal candidiasis. The key virulence factor for tissue invasion is its ability to undergo morphological transition from yeast to hyphal form (germ tube formation). Hyphae can penetrate epithelial cells and escape phagocytosis. Ergosterol is a target for antifungals. Capsule production is virulence factor for Cryptococcus. Melanin production is important for Cryptococcus and other melanized fungi.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female patient presents with photosensitivity, malar rash, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640), anti-dsDNA positive. She develops a diffuse non-scarring alopecia. What type of hair loss is this?
questions.exp: SLE-associated diffuse alopecia is called 'lupus hair' which refers to fragile, short hairs at the frontal hairline that break off easily. It is non-scarring and reflects active systemic disease. Anagen effluvium occurs with chemotherapy (proximal hair shaft narrowing). Telogen effluvium is stress-related. Discoid lupus can cause scarring alopecia but this patient has systemic (not discoid) disease.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly, telangiectatic papule on his nose with central ulceration that has been slowly growing for 2 years. The lesion has rolled borders. Histology shows peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with retraction artifact. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for a 1.5 cm lesion on the nose?
questions.exp: This is a basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (high-risk H-zone). For BCCs in high-risk locations (central face including nose, periorbital, periauricular, scalp), Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (~99%) with maximal tissue conservation. Standard excision with 4mm margins has ~95% cure rate but is not preferred for H-zone lesions due to recurrence risk and cosmetic concerns.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension develops a lichenoid drug eruption. Which of the following drugs is NOT typically associated with lichenoid drug eruptions?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (retinoid) does not cause lichenoid drug eruptions. Classic causes of lichenoid drug eruptions include thiazide diuretics, gold, antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine), penicillamine, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and NSAIDs. The eruption resembles lichen planus clinically and histologically but characteristically has eosinophils and parakeratosis on histology, which is uncommon in true LP.

questions.q: A neonate is born with thick, plate-like scales covering the entire body, ectropion, and eclabium. The baby was encased in a'collodion membrane' at birth. Electron microscopy of skin shows abnormal lamellar granule morphology. This is most likely:
questions.exp: Lamellar ichthyosis presents with a collodion baby phenotype at birth, evolving to large, dark, plate-like scales with ectropion and eclabium. It is caused by mutations in TGM1 (transglutaminase-1), ABCA12, CYP4F22, and others. EM shows abnormal lamellar granules. Epidermolytic ichthyosis shows epidermolysis (blistering) at birth. XLI is caused by steroid sulfatase deficiency with fine brownish scales. Netherton syndrome has bamboo hair.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and calcinosis. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. Which internal organ complication is she most at risk for?
questions.exp: This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) / CREST syndrome with anti-centromere antibodies (ACA). lcSSc is specifically associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) as the most serious internal complication, occurring in 10-15% of patients. Pulmonary fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis are more characteristic of diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) with anti-Scl-70/anti-topoisomerase I antibodies.

questions.q: A 16-year-old patient presents with crops of vesicles and erosions in a herpetiform distribution on the back, shoulders, and buttocks. There is intense pruritus. Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin would most likely show:
opts: IgG and C3 in intercellular spaces
Granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae
questions.exp: This is dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), the skin manifestation of celiac disease. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae (pathognomonic). IIF shows anti-epidermal transglutaminase 3 (TG3) antibodies. Linear IgG at DEJ = BP. Intercellular IgG = pemphigus vulgaris. Linear IgA at DEJ = linear IgA bullous dermatosis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man who works in a coal mine presents with black pigmentation of the skin, particularly in sun-exposed areas, along with nail hyperpigmentation. He has no systemic symptoms. Which chemical is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Chronic arsenic exposure causes raindrop pigmentation (macular hyperpigmentation interspersed with hypopigmented macules), Mees' lines on nails, keratoses on palms and soles (arsenical keratoses), and predisposes to Bowen's disease and squamous cell carcinoma. Coal mine workers can be exposed to arsenic compounds. Lead causes Burton's line on gums. Mercury causes acrodynia. Chromium causes contact dermatitis and ulceration.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male with long-standing atopic dermatitis develops patches of erythema with indurated plaques, covered with fine scale, on the trunk. Biopsy shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses. TCR gene rearrangement is positive. CD4:CD8 ratio is inverted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Early stages show patch/plaque lesions with epidermotropism and Pautrier microabscesses (collections of atypical CD4+ T-cells within epidermis). Sézary syndrome is the leukemic variant with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and >1000 Sézary cells/mm3 in blood. CD4:CD8 ratio is elevated (not inverted) in MF (CD4+ cells predominate).

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active female presents with painless, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like growths on the vulva and perianal region. Which HPV serotypes are most commonly responsible?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused predominantly by HPV 6 and 11 (low-risk types), which have low oncogenic potential. HPV 16, 18, 31, 33 are high-risk oncogenic types associated with cervical, vulvar, anal, and penile cancers. HPV 2 and 4 cause common warts (verruca vulgaris) on hands/feet.

questions.q: A patient is undergoing patch testing for suspected contact dermatitis. A 2+ reaction is read at 96 hours. This would appear as:
opts: Strong erythema, papules, and small vesicles
Extreme reaction with bullae and ulceration
Coalescing vesicles with erythema beyond the test site
questions.exp: International Contact Dermatitis Research Group (ICDRG) grading: 1+ = erythema, infiltration, possibly papules; 2+ = erythema, infiltration, papules, small vesicles; 3+ = erythema, infiltration, papules, coalescing vesicles; extreme (++) with bullae/ulceration is sometimes graded separately or as 3+. A 2+ reaction indicates strong contact allergy with small discrete vesicles.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, red, indurated plaque with central ulceration on his ear that has grown from 1cm to 4cm in 6 weeks. Histology shows moderate to poorly differentiated SCC with perineural invasion. This is classified as high-risk SCC. Which feature is NOT considered a high-risk factor for SCC?
questions.exp: High-risk features for cutaneous SCC include: tumor diameter >2cm, depth >2mm or Clark level IV/V, poorly differentiated histology, perineural invasion, location on ear or lip, arising in a scar/chronic wound, immunosuppression, and recurrent tumors. Superficial depth (<2mm) is actually a low-risk feature associated with better prognosis. Breslow thickness is a melanoma staging parameter, but depth >2mm applies to SCC risk stratification.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with oval brownish-red macules and thin plaques on the trunk that urticate on rubbing (Darier's sign positive). Bone marrow biopsy shows aggregates of mast cells. Serum tryptase is 28 ng/mL. The c-KIT mutation (D816V) is detected. This confirms:
questions.exp: The WHO criteria for systemic mastocytosis (SM) require 1 major criterion (multifocal dense infiltrates of mast cells ≥15 cells in BM/organs) plus 1 minor criterion, OR 3 minor criteria. Minor criteria include: >25% atypical spindle-shaped mast cells, c-KIT D816V mutation, CD2/CD25 co-expression, serum tryptase >20 ng/mL. This patient has BM involvement, elevated tryptase, and KIT mutation = SM. Serum tryptase >20 is not sufficient alone for cutaneous-only disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops photosensitivity with burning sensation on sun-exposed areas. Phototesting shows abnormal minimal erythema dose (MED) to UVA. The action spectrum is mainly UVA (320-400nm). Urine examination shows elevated porphyrins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) presents in childhood/young adults with immediate burning/stinging pain on sun exposure (within minutes), UVA-mediated. Caused by ferrochelatase deficiency with elevated protoporphyrin IX in RBCs, plasma, and stool. PCT presents with photosensitive blistering, skin fragility, milia, hypertrichosis, and elevated uroporphyrin in urine. PMLE is delayed-type (hours after exposure) with papulovesicular lesions. Solar urticaria is immediate but urticarial.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with a linear, verrucous epidermal nevus following Blaschko's lines on the left leg since birth. The lesion is pruritic. Histopathology shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis. This is consistent with:
questions.exp: ILVEN is a type of epidermal nevus with persistent pruritus and a psoriasiform/lichenoid histology with alternating parakeratosis and orthokeratosis. It follows Blaschko's lines, is usually present from birth/early childhood, and is refractory to treatment. Linear lichen planus would have lichenoid histology with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. Linear psoriasis is rare and would show classic psoriasiform changes without the linear Blaschko's pattern.

questions.q: A patient with tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is started on terbinafine 250mg daily for 12 weeks. Which of the following statements about terbinafine is CORRECT?
opts: It inhibits squalene epoxidase causing squalene accumulation
It requires dose adjustment in mild renal impairment
questions.exp: Terbinafine is an allylamine antifungal that inhibits squalene epoxidase (not 14α-demethylase, which is the target of azoles). This causes squalene accumulation within fungal cells and ergosterol deficiency, leading to cell death. Terbinafine is fungicidal (not fungistatic). It is primarily hepatically metabolized; no dose adjustment needed for mild-moderate renal impairment, but used cautiously in severe renal/hepatic impairment.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male presents with hypopigmented macules and papules on the trunk with fine adherent scale. KOH preparation shows a mixture of short, curved hyphae and round budding cells ('spaghetti and meatballs' appearance). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now classified as multiple Malassezia species). The pathognomonic KOH finding is the 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern: short curved hyphae (spaghetti) and clusters of round spores (meatballs). The yeast phase is lipophilic and requires olive oil overlay on culture. Candida shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. Dermatophytes show septate hyphae only.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man on long-term dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops sudden onset hemolytic anemia. G6PD deficiency is confirmed. Which metabolite of dapsone is responsible for the hemolysis?
questions.exp: Dapsone is converted by cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP2C9, CYP3A4) to dapsone hydroxylamine (DDS-NHOH), which is the metabolite responsible for methemoglobin formation and hemolytic anemia. In G6PD-deficient patients, this risk is markedly increased because G6PD is essential for regenerating NADPH needed to reduce methemoglobin back to hemoglobin. Monoacetyldapsone (MADDS) is the principal N-acetylated metabolite formed by NAT2.

questions.q: During a dermoscopy examination, a 2.5cm lesion on the back of a 45-year-old shows atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, and blue-white veil. These findings are most consistent with:
questions.exp: Blue-white veil is a highly specific dermoscopic feature of melanoma, representing compact orthokeratosis overlying a diffuse melanin-containing area. Combined with atypical pigment network (irregular meshwork) and irregular streaks (pseudopods/radial streaming), these are major melanoma criteria. Compound nevus shows regular pigment network. SK shows milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings. Dermatofibroma shows central white scar-like patch and peripheral delicate network.

questions.q: A 40-year-old construction worker presents with palpable purpura on both lower extremities for 3 weeks following a streptococcal throat infection. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) with fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls and nuclear dust. DIF shows IgA deposits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is the most common vasculitis in children but occurs in adults too. It is characterized by palpable purpura (typically lower limbs), arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, often triggered by upper respiratory infection. DIF showing IgA deposits in vessel walls is pathognomonic. MPA is ANCA-associated. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis shows IgG/IgM deposits. PAN affects medium vessels and skin shows livedo, nodules, and ulcers.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy develops sudden onset of multiple tender, erythematous nodules on the face and limbs, along with fever and worsening of existing lesions. CBC shows neutrophilia. This reaction type is mediated by:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL / Type 2 lepra reaction) occurs in LL and BL leprosy. It is mediated by immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) deposition with complement activation and neutrophil recruitment. TNF-α is a key cytokine. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate with immune complexes. Reversal reaction (Type 1) involves delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV). Treatment of ENL: thalidomide (drug of choice) or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with painless swelling of the left testis for 6 months. He has a history of a painless genital ulcer 2 years ago that healed spontaneously. VDRL is reactive at 1:128, FTA-ABS is positive. This patient is in which stage of syphilis?
questions.exp: Orchitis/testicular gumma is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis (gummatous syphilis), occurring 1-10 years after the initial infection. The gumma is a destructive granulomatous lesion that can affect any organ (skin, bones, liver, testes). The history of a healed painless ulcer (primary chancre) supports syphilis. High-titer VDRL with positive FTA-ABS confirms active syphilitic infection. Tertiary syphilis is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 weeks.
